entry.title: docs: make room for NonCommercial source material, outside git (#36)
entry.content:
docs: make room for NonCommercial source material, outside git (#36)

The open textbook the first course follows turns out to be CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, not
plain CC as THIRD-PARTY.md claimed. The NC clause is one-way incompatible with
the CC BY-SA course content: BY-SA permits commercial use and NC forbids it, so
no amount of transformation relicenses it.

That does not make the book useless -- reading a textbook and then writing your
own exercises is what a textbook is for. It means the extracted material has to
live on one side of a line a later contributor cannot cross by accident.

So `reference/` exists, with everything under it gitignored, and its README says
plainly that the reason is the licence and not the file size -- because the
extract is a few hundred kilobytes, and "it's small, let's just commit it" is
exactly the thought that would undo this.

Corrects the THIRD-PARTY row: structure only. Which grammar point precedes which
is a fact about teaching a language and following it is fine; the sentences,
tables and passages are not ours to ship.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

entry.title: feat(content): rank distractors by shared stem and by how common a wo…
entry.content:
feat(content): rank distractors by shared stem and by how common a word is (#34)

Closes the paradigm and frequency half of the distractor work.

`morphology` -- a candidate sharing a stem with the answer -- is the hardest
kind of option to eliminate without knowing the grammar, because for a Romance
language it IS the conjugation paradigm. On the real corpus it produces exactly
the sets the exercise is testing: `passada` against `passado`, `ainda` against
`ainda assim`, `saio` against `saem` and `saímos`. 570 of 3360 distractors now
come from it.

It carries two thresholds and both are load-bearing. A short answer has no stem
to share: `o` and `ontem` agree on one letter by coincidence, and honouring that
ranked `ontem`, `outubro` and `onze` above `as` as options for an article --
measurably worse than no signal. A long answer needs only two characters, since
`sa|io` against `sa|em` is a real paradigm. A length floor separates the two
cases; a bare count of shared characters cannot, and my first attempt at one
made the article cards worse.

Frequency ranking uses `wordfreq` behind an optional extra. Its absence changes
the order of options within a tier, never which are eligible or how they are
labelled, so a course built with it and one built without differ in polish
rather than correctness. The language comes from `course.l2.code`; the engine
holds no language knowledge of its own.

`mlconjug3` was the planned source for paradigms and is not usable: it fails to
import under scikit-learn 1.9 (`No module named '_loss'`, its pickled models
predate the move) and pulls 232MB for the privilege. Recorded in THIRD-PARTY.md
so the next person does not spend the afternoon I did.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

entry.title: feat(content): precomputed distractors, and serving the choice form (…
entry.content:
feat(content): precomputed distractors, and serving the choice form (#33)

Closes #32.

Multiple choice was refused outright because there was nothing honest to put
beside the answer. There is now: a `distractors` table, computed at content sync
from two sources -- the note's own `distractors:` field, which is the author
saying "this is the mistake I expect" and beats any heuristic, and other notes'
answers to the same field of the same note type, nearest in length, from the
same unit before the wider course.

This is a scheduling concern, not a rendering one. Options that can be
eliminated without knowing anything mean the card is answered correctly whatever
the learner knows, which inflates measured accuracy -- and accuracy is what
opens the new-material gate. A multiple choice with filler options would make
the app introduce material faster than anyone can absorb it. So `choice` is
capability-gated on having real distractors and is simply not offered otherwise,
and `validate` reports the cards that lose the form so the author knows.

Generation is deterministic. Anything random would churn the table on every
content rebuild and make a content diff unreadable; the shuffle happens when the
card is served.

On the real corpus: 560 of 676 cards resolve a full set, and a session now
serves choice, typein, wordbank and flashcard rather than typein alone.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

entry.title: fix(import): never overwrite a card answered in this engine (#31)
entry.content:
fix(import): never overwrite a card answered in this engine (#31)

Re-importing overwrote every `card_state` row unconditionally. That was harmless
while the predecessor was the only place studying happened and this database was
a reproducible copy of it. It stops being harmless the moment anyone answers a
card here: the import would silently revert a real answer to the state it was
imported in, which is the same failure the append-only review log exists to
prevent, arriving through a different door.

Imported history is stamped `sm2-legacy`, so any other algo in the log is an
answer given here. Those cards keep their state and are reported; everything
else still refreshes. A dry run says what it would keep without writing, since
that is the number worth seeing before running it for real.

Proven on the running instance, not only in tests: a card answered twice here
went from seen 3 to 5, a full re-import from the predecessor left it at 5, and
two card states were reported as kept.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

entry.title: fix(policies): hold a note's siblings back from today, do not requeue…
entry.content:
fix(policies): hold a note's siblings back from today, do not requeue them (#29)

* fix(policies): hold a note's siblings back from today, do not requeue them

Closes #27.

`bury_siblings` moved a note's extra cards to the end of the queue. That reads
as burying and is not: the whole queue ships in one `/api/session` batch, so
both siblings reached the learner in the same sitting anyway -- the exact thing
ADR-0001 requires this to prevent, since the second card is then answered from
the first rather than from memory.

Held back now means not served today. The card keeps its due date, unpenalised,
and comes up in the next session; over three days a three-card note is seen
three times, once each. That is Anki's semantics for the same reason.

The count is reported on `/api/session` rather than left silent: a queue shorter
than the stated debt deserves a visible cause.

No effect on the imported corpus, where every legacy type maps to a single-
template note type and no note has siblings. It bites the moment content uses
`vocab` or `picture`, which is what the sample course already does -- serving 7
cards from 4 notes before this, 4 after.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

* test(web): drive the session until the plan is exhausted, not twice

The end-to-end session test assumed two passes covered every card. That held
while one note meant one card. Holding siblings back to a later session makes
the number vary -- a two-card note needs a further round before its second card
is introduced at all -- so the test now runs until the queue is empty or turns
to consolidation, and asserts every card was reached.

Caught by CI, not locally: the failure only appears once the branch is merged
with a main that already has the presentation ladder.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

---------

entry.title: feat(presenters): ask a never-answered card in a recognition form (#26)
entry.content:
feat(presenters): ask a never-answered card in a recognition form (#26)

The recognition-to-production ladder from the predecessor's render_as()
becomes a Presenter, so "how a card is asked" is a policy with a registry
rather than a chain of ifs in a view. A card with seen == 0 is asked in a
recognition form -- a word bank for a sentence, a multiple choice for a
word -- and in its declared, productive form from the second encounter on.

Keyed on `seen`, never on `reps`. `reps` is reset to zero by every lapse,
so a genuinely hard card would be demoted to multiple choice forever and
never once be asked to produce anything.

`choice` is not renderable in this build: it cannot be served without
putting the answer beside its distractors while the question is open. So
the ladder degrades to the declared form whenever the easier rung is not
on offer, and PresentationContext now carries the renderable forms and the
answer's length -- the shape signal that decides which rung is meant.

The web layer asks the presenter through serialize.served_form(), with the
card's state read before the answer is recorded, so the review log keeps
the form the learner actually saw.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

entry.title: fix(web): serve opaque handles, never card ids (#28)
entry.content:
fix(web): serve opaque handles, never card ids (#28)

Closes #17.

Card ids are scheduling keys and are authored from the material: a note teaching
`obrigado` is called `obrigado`, so its production card is `obrigado#produce`.
The id therefore IS the answer. Measured on the first real course imported into
this engine: 167 of 676 cards, a quarter of the corpus, would have been
answerable by reading the network tab.

Filtering fields cannot fix this, because an id is not a field. It has to reach
the client so an answer can be posted back for it. So the client stops seeing
it: each card gets a random per-run token, the server resolves the token when
the answer arrives, and neither the card id nor the note id appears in a payload
any more.

Handles are regenerated on every start. An open question at restart therefore
resolves to nothing and the client refetches, which is the right outcome anyway
since the content may have changed under it.

The strict xfail that recorded this gap is removed rather than left to report a
fixed bug as a failure. The web tests that asserted the served id equals the card
id were asserting the leak; they now resolve the handle and additionally assert
that the two differ.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

entry.title: fix(policies): spend the lesson budget on lesson material, order the …
entry.content:
fix(policies): spend the lesson budget on lesson material, order the debt (#25)

Two bugs in the daily queue, both in policies/daily.py.

The lesson introduction cap was charged by every card met for the first
time today, back catalogue included, so a day with a real backlog could
shrink -- or close -- the exemption that exists precisely so the lesson
just attended never waits. It is counted with a new store query,
lesson_first_seen_on, restricted to notes whose lesson is inside the
LESSON_FRESH_DAYS window: the same window lesson_is_fresh uses, so what
spends the budget is exactly what the budget is for.

scheduled_cards had no ORDER BY, and build_session's stable sort by due
date leaves ties in whatever order the rows arrived in -- the planner's
choice, free to change under a SQLite upgrade, an added index or an
ANALYZE. Most of a real backlog is ties: 32 cards over 3 dates in the
snapshot. It now orders by n.unit, n.ord, c.id -- content order, the
tie-break introduction_order already uses, closed by a card id that is
unique and never changes.

The parity tests that pinned both divergences are updated: the lesson
budget now matches the predecessor exactly, and the due-order class
asserts a deterministic difference (content order against the order rows
happen to come out of the predecessor's items table) instead of asserting
that the engine has no order at all. The real-snapshot test additionally
checks, element for element, that the engine's owed list is decided by
the schedule and the content and by nothing else.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

entry.title: fix(ci): repair environment bootstrap and language-neutrality check
entry.content:
fix(ci): repair environment bootstrap and language-neutrality check

Both jobs failed on the first push, for unrelated reasons.

`uv pip install --system` refuses to install: the runner's system Python is
externally managed (PEP 668), and `uv python install` does not change which
interpreter `--system` resolves to. Create a project virtualenv and run the
tools through `uv run` instead.

The language-neutrality job flagged its own documentation. It grepped the source
for target-language words, and `core/protocols.py` says, in a comment, that the
engine folds accents "because a course asked it to, not because it knows about
Portuguese" — the rule being explained, reported as the rule being broken.

Replaced with `scripts/check_language_neutral.py`, which parses the source and
inspects identifiers and non-docstring string literals, ignoring comments and
docstrings entirely. That matches what the rule actually says: an identifier or a
default value encoding one language's behaviour is a violation; prose about the
policy is not. Verified in both directions — it passes the current engine and
catches a planted `{"vocabulario": 0.5}` and a `grade_portugues()`.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>
